Bill Kirchner

Bill Kirchner was born in 1953 in Youngstown, Ohio. He has made a mark in the jazz world as a saxophonist, composer/arranger, jazz historian, producer, educator, and radio personality. Bill’s most creative work has been performed and recorded by the Bill Kirchner Nonet. He remains active as an educator and composer despite the onset of significant physical limitations.
Bill was interviewed via Zoom on June 4, 2021 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

My name is Monk Rowe for the Fillius Jazz Archive at Hamilton College and I’m very pleased to have Bill Kirchner with me today. And I had the little stumbling block of how to start with you because I’ve been reading some of the interviews you’ve done and most people say a similar thing and that’s you’ve worn so many hats, which hat should I concentrate on?
I couldn’t begin to tell you that. I’m the worst person to ask.

Yes exactly. But I did want — I had a thought — I do some arranging and I have over the years, in fact our career paths have some similarities. And I’m currently working on an arrangement. And on the way up today in the car it was going through my head, sort of what to do next, where am I, how am I going to end it. And I wonder if it’s something similar for you when you’re working on a piece of music. Is it constantly in your head until you finish it?

Interesting question. Yes, short answer. Yeah I think it becomes something almost like an obsession. And sometimes, I don’t have a car anymore but I remember when I did have a car I remember some of the best ideas I got was when I was in the car, or you know, other bizarre places like in the shower or whatever you know. The ideas come when they come and there’s no predicting that.

Isn’t that so interesting, you don’t have to be sitting at the piano or score paper or Finale or whatever, they just seem to have this way of presenting themselves. And I know I’ve lost some ideas — walking the dog and I get this idea and yeah, by the time I get home it may be gone.

Well you know Duke Ellington used to carry a little notebook on him at all times so he could write down ideas when they came to him, no matter when they came or where he was when they came, which I think is a good idea, especially if you were Duke Ellington.

When you, let’s suppose I commissioned you to write a chart on a song that’s been done to death — let’s say “All of Me.” For some reason I want an arrangement of “All of Me” for a full sized jazz ensemble. Can you describe — and maybe you say, “What about © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
something else.” No, I’m insistent, I want “All of Me.” Can you tell me how you might approach this trying to get something different out of this tune?
Well I should point out as part of this, are you familiar with Fred Sturm’s book? Composing/arranging book?
Somewhat, yes.

He did that very thing. He commissioned a bunch of great arrangers to do charts on “All of Me” including Manny Albam and Bob Brookmeyer and Bill Holman and others. And they all came up with different slants on it, some of them outrageously outside, like Brookmeyer. So it’s interesting that you should mention that, and pick that particular tune, because indeed it’s been done for precisely the reason that you’re talking about. Anyway to try to answer your question, I guess I would begin by asking about the band that I was writing for, about the people who were playing, what their strengths and weaknesses are, what their interests are, what they do best. That would give me a clue about how to approach it and, you know, the more personal that you can get the better off you are and the more distinctive your end product is going to be I think. So that’s where I would start is just asking who are your best soloists, what do they do best? And then take it from there. I remember about twenty-some years ago I got a commission from the U.S. Air Force Airmen of Note. They said Pete BarenBregge, who was the leader of the band at the time, you know, just gave me a commission and said, “Write whatever you want.” And so I mean we’re talking about a band in this case that’s been in existence since 1950 that has a book of thousands of charts. And I said, “Well what don’t you have a lot of?” And he said, “Shuffles.” So I ended up doing a kind of a jazz-rock shuffle. And so I mean that’s an example of just trying to find something that worked for them that they would have use for that hadn’t been done to death. And it came out pretty well, at least I was happy with it. I don’t know if they ever play it but I’ve had several performances of it otherwise with various college bands here and in Europe since then, and they played it well, so I know it worked.
I would have been so happy if that had been me because I dearly love a shuffle.
Yeah, sure. It’s kind of an infectious groove but you know it’s very rhythmic. I mean the whole point of the thing is rhythm of course.
Well that anticipated a question, because you were assigned a groove so to speak. What comes next? Does the melody come next or the chord sequence or the form?

Well you know what I did? In 1989 and ’91 I spent two years studying with Bob Brookmeyer and Manny Albam in the BMI Jazz Composers’ Workshop. And they taught us a technique called “Pitch Modules” where you take three note pitch cells and use it to develop raw material from which to write music. And I teach it to all my composing/arranging students and I tell them, tongue in cheekedly, that using this © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

technique is much better than waiting to break-up with your significant other for an inspiration. So in this case, when I wrote this chart for the Airmen of Note, and often when I’m writing, you know, original music, I’ll use this “Pitch Module” technique just to develop raw material. And it can, from that can arise melodies or harmonies. You can use these rows of notes that come from the pitch module to derive whatever you want, in essence. So in essence what happened with that chart, the Airmen of Note, is I came up with the melody and I came up with some countermelodies and I came up with some harmonies as a result. So after you do the work you go through and just find stuff that you like and let nature take its course.
Can I assume that somewhere along the line you moved, when writing scores, from a score paper pad to Finale or Sibelius or something like that?

Ut uh. I can’t write on the computer. I still have to write on score paper, and then I have a copyist quote unquote who’s adept on you know Finale and Sibelius who then, I’ll just give the score to and he can load it in for me. I mean I know a number of composers and arrangers who are like me, who have just never made the transition.
Yeah, I don’t know if you know Dave Rivello at Eastman?
Oh, Dave and I are both from Youngstown, Ohio.
I’ll be darned.
We held — our first arranging teacher was Sam DeAngelo who was my high school band director, rest his soul. He died a couple of years ago. But Dave and I had Sam for our first arranging teacher.

I went to his house to interview him and I was so pleased to see he had this whole setup with, you know, a big like draftsman table and he had the score paper and so I asked him about that. He said, “Well there’s something about the physical act of choosing a note with a pencil and putting it on the paper. It’s like you’re much more committed than just putting something with a mouse that you can easily go back and take away I guess.”

Well in my case I’m a techno-putz. So I just can’t deal with the idea of having some mechanical thing be between me and the act of putting the notes on the score you know. If I lose an idea because I’m fumbling with trying to do the mechanics then I’ve lost something and I don’t want to take that chance. I don’t know, I have a low frustration threshold with stuff like that. I tried to learn Finale and I tried to learn Sibelius and it just drove me nuts. I just couldn’t handle it.

Well as we go along we have more and more in common. I want to take you back, you mentioned Mr. DeAngelo, and can you recall the feeling or your reaction to the first time you heard one of your early arrangements played?
Oh yeah. I wrote my first big band chart for Sam when I was in high school. We had a quote stage band. And he was a piano player and an arranger and he wrote charts for the © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-

band on things like “Comin’ Home Baby” and “So What.” I mean this was late 60s, early 70s. And I mean for the time, that was very hip for any kind of school band, college or high school. I mean this was a high school band. So the fact that he was writing charts for us was, this was so cool. So I got interested in writing and he encouraged me to write and I wrote this chart on “A Taste of Honey,” you know the Bobby Scott tune? So that was my first chart for a big band. And we played it and it wasn’t bad. I mean I didn’t know a lot about voicing for horns and stuff like that, but I knew enough to come up with something that sounded halfway decent. And it was a great thrill you know, you can imagine, you come up with something like that that’s your own, it’s a whole new part of you that you didn’t know you had and like bam, there it is.
Did any of the players in the band provide some feedback like, “I can’t play that. That’s really awkward.”
No, no, nothing. Everything seemed to lay okay. Nobody said anything to the contrary to me anyway.

Okay. Was there something, I read an anecdote about you hearing the Ellington band and how much an impression — I’m also wondering if there was something in your household, LPs or radio or something that helped set you on your eventual path?
Well do you want me to tell the story about the Ellington band etcetera, etcetera? Shall I start there?

Well yeah, I’m more curious because I’ve been interested in how every generation has their high tech things that their entertainment is delivered through. And when we think back to, you and I are close in age and if we think back to our formative years, the high tech at that time, so what was in your household that you might have heard music from?

Well I mean aside from television, in the late 50s if you recall there was a sudden surge of jazz oriented scores for TV cop shows, like “Peter Gunn,” “Mr. Lucky,” “Johnny Staccato,” “Checkmates,” all these forgotten TV shows that people like Henry Mancini and John Williams and Pete Rugolo and Johnny Mandel and others were writing scores for. So I heard this music, beginning with “Peter Gunn” when I was about five years old and this was some of the first music I can remember hearing and some of the first jazz I can remember hearing. And it all just hit me remarkably hard. Just the harmony, all these hip harmonies, and the rhythms of course, and of course all these scores were played by some of the hippest jazz musicians in LA at the time. So that was a big exposure to jazz and to music, and also my parents were very low tech. I mean they didn’t even have LPs until I got seriously interested in music and they finally bought a stereo, you know, to play LPs. But for much of my childhood all we had was the 45 RPM record player to play. So they had a handful of 45s, Glenn Miller things, Tex Beneke, you know. Actually there was a, do you remember a piano player named Lou Stein? © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
I do not.

He was a really good jazz piano player who was active in the 40s, 50s, until maybe twenty years ago, active in New York, played with a lot of people. And one of the 45s that my mother had was the thing that Lou had, it was kind of a fluke hit called “Soft Sands.” And so I remember playing that a lot of times and I memorized the melody and could play it on my horns, on clarinet to begin with. So fast forward, oh God, ‘til the late 1980s and I end up on this club date, by club date I’m using the musician’s term, you know weddings, bar mitzvahs, private parties, that sort. So I ended up on a club date in Connecticut with Lou Stein. So we were in the middle of this gig and we’re just playing dinner music or something. And I said, “Could we play ‘Soft Sands’?” I thought his jaw was going to hit the floor you know. It was great fun. So we played “Soft Sands.” You know I’m sure he’d never gotten a request for that in his life.
I’ll be darned. That’s a great moment. What about radio? Did it have any impact on you?

Oh yeah. Well my parents would listen to the radio every morning when we were getting ready for school and all that stuff, and it was AM radio at the time. I mean the stations they listened to, my parents were very non-rock & roll. They listened to mainstream adult pop music. So I mean they would have on the radio what the records of the time were, maybe Sinatra things or Tony Bennett or Barbra Streisand, or whatever was in the air at the time. So I got exposed to a lot of that. And you know I mean I had good ears and a good retentive memory so I could end up playing these things on my horn and kind of absorbing stuff that was in the air and then eventually, I guess that’s what generated my interest in arranging was just hearing all this stuff on the radio, a lot of which was backed by big band.
Can I guess that your parents looked askance at a music career?

Good guess. Oh yeah. I mean no they didn’t want me to have a career as a musician, although I mean they did encourage my interest in music. I mean they paid for music lessons for me for years, and I should tell this story, going back to the Ellington. In 1965 I was just short of my twelfth birthday and I had this neophyte’s interest in jazz. So there was a three day jazz festival in Pittsburgh at the civic arena that George Wein was producing. And Pittsburgh is about an hour or so’s drive from Youngstown. So for my upcoming twelfth birthday my parents gave me an early birthday present and said we’ll take you to this festival on a Saturday night. So we went to Pittsburgh to the civic arena, and the bill for the one night, it was a Saturday night, the opening act was this local guy, a piano player named Walt Harper with his group; and then Earl Hines with a trio; Carmen McRae with Norman Simmons’ trio; Stan Getz’s quartet with Gary Burton, Steve Swallow and Roy Haynes; John Coltrane’s quartet with McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison and Elvin Jones; and the Ellington band with Billy Strayhorn as a guest because © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

Strayhorn was from Pittsburgh, as was Earl Hines. So this was kind of a homecoming for both of them. So this was the bill for one night. And I mean that was the night that basically set me on my career path, even though my parents didn’t realize it at the time nor would they have approved if they’d known it, but I mean that really set me on my career path I mean as far as solidifying a serious interest in jazz. Up to that point I’d been doing my best to listen to top 40 radio to conform to the interest of my schoolmates. But after that top 40 radio just went down the toilet. I couldn’t care less after that. I started using whatever allowance money I had to buy LPs. My parents bought a stereo that I could play the LPs on, and other than that, you know there were some syndicated jazz radio shows like Sid Mark in Philadelphia had a syndicated jazz radio show that I would listen to on Saturday nights. And there was a 50,000 watt clear channel station in Rochester, New York, WHAM, that had a five hour jazz show from midnight to five in the morning that I would listen to on my transistor radio, especially when I was on holidays from school. I would just lie in bed with my transistor. This is late 60s, early 70s. And there were two different DJs. The first guy was a guy named Bill Ardis, and then his successor was a guy named Harry Abraham. And they played really hip stuff, you know whatever the new LP releases were. I mean I heard, I remember one night I was listening to the radio and this kind of funk type thing came on and I was wondering what is this? Is this Cannonball Adderley or something? And it turned out to be Miles Davis from “Miles in the Sky” doing that tune called “Stuff” which was the first time Herbie Hancock recorded on a Fender Rhodes. So I heard that on Harry Abraham’s show. So I heard, I guess at that point I had found outlets that were — even in Youngstown, Ohio I could hear what was going on.

In retrospect, at the risk of sounding, you know, oh back in my day, there was something magical about finding these things. And you know you had a little transistor radio and saving up money to get LPs and then reading the liner notes as you listen to the record. It was like a whole experience.

Oh yeah. Yeah for sure. Well including the liner notes. I mean written by people like, well also I started reading DownBeat. You know I was reading all this stuff by people like Dan Morgenstern and Ira Gitler and Martin Williams, all of whom later became friends and colleagues of mine. So that was a big part of my education was reading this stuff that these people and others were writing at the time.

It’s interesting that you heard John Coltrane at that point in your life. I believe I read something where you were talking about early on you were trying to do the John Coltrane thing but you had no direction to it. I’m not sure that’s the exact quote.

Close enough. No I was just trying to play as many notes as I could with no real sense of, you know, I mean I certainly didn’t understand Coltrane’s harmonic concept at the time. I © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

mean I was just trying to play a lot of notes. So when I got to New York in 1971 and I started studying with Lee Konitz, the very first lesson I went to leave for, and I studied with him for two years, he handed me a Frank Sinatra album, “Songs for Swinging Lovers” and he said, “Okay take this home and learn to sing along with Sinatra, exactly the way he sings, on one of these tunes, with all the inflections and the rhythmic feel and whatever. And it’s a great exercise for anybody. I mean all his life, and I knew Lee, we were friends until he died basically. For his practice routine for the rest of his life, I mean he would sing along with Sinatra records. That was an important part of his practice routine. And it’s a great exercise. It gets you away from the horn and just puts you kind of in direct contact with the music without any instrument between you and the music.

For me it begs the question, sometimes you read comments about jazz and I think they’re usually written, not the musician writers, the non-musician writers, who say jazz musicians play what they feel. And I’ve had this debate with myself about how much emotion is connected to improvisation. Is it driven by emotion and feeling or is it driven by more theoretical knowledge? I know what chord I’m playing here and I know that this will sound out, this will sound in. I’m not sure that’s a question but it’s — I’ll let you try to deal with it.

Yeah I probably, my answer would be it’s all of the above. I mean certainly emotion should have an important bearing on it because if it isn’t then why are we doing it? But also I mean you have to have a solid either theoretical knowledge or some kind of instinctual thing about the music. I mean somebody, there are some great players like for example Chet Baker knew nothing about harmony in a theoretical sense but he had great ears. So you know I mean he had his own kind of knowledge. You know it was an instinctual thing and it wasn’t based on music theory but it was knowledge nonetheless. So you know if you have the instinctual knowledge or the theoretical knowledge of some sort combined with the emotional thing, that that’s where substantial music comes from I would think. That’s been my experience anyway.
In the years, let’s say the early 70s, I think you had returned to New York.
I went for the first time. I went to college in New York from ’71 to ’75.
Okay. Did you go to clubs as often as you could afford let’s say, and do you recall hearing any particular group or individual that just sort of blew you away?

Everything man. I mean look I arrived in New York in the fall of 1971 and in the first six months I was in New York I can tell you who I heard. And you have to remember that I went to clubs as much as I could on my limited college kid’s budget. But there was also a lot of free stuff going on, free meaning no charge. But the first six months I heard Lee Konitz playing with a minimalist named Lamont Young in the Metropolitan Museum actually; then I heard Elvin Jones’ quartet in a little auditorium on the upper west side © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

with Joe Farrell and Dave Liebman and Gene Perla; I heard the Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band at the Village Vanguard, this was the first of a number of times I heard them at the Vanguard; I heard Chick Corea and Return to Forever, their first gig at the Village Vanguard, this was the Return to Forever with Joe Farrell and Flora Purim and Stanley Clarke, and I heard Airto Moreira, this was their first gig ever and it was one of the greatest nights of live music I have ever heard, as good as the records were that they made. In person they were just stunning. I heard Charles Mingus’ all-star big band at Philharmonic Hall with Lee Konitz, Gerry Mulligan, Gene Ammons, Milt Hinton, Joe Chambers, Jon Faddis. I heard Sonny Rollins at the Vanguard with Albert Dailey, Larry Ridley and David Lee. This was the first six months you know. And then after that well I was in school. There was a lot of, as I said, there were a lot of free concerts going on. There was this place on 55th Street called the New York Jazz Museum that opened up while I was in college. They would have Sunday afternoon concerts for free. And I heard a bunch of people there. I heard Howard McGhee and Joe Carroll. I heard Hank Mobley. I heard Thad and Mel with the quintet with Billy Harper and George Mraz and Walter Norris. Jimmy Guiffre. You know this was all for free you know. You could just go on a Sunday afternoon.
Were you ever tempted at that time to call up Mom and Dad and say, “Listen, I’m not going to major anymore in what I’m doing, I have to be a musician.”

No. I didn’t have the guts. Plus I was, you know, this was my excuse for being in New York. So I mean I was studying with Konitz for a couple of years and then I started studying for a couple of years with Harold Danko, who by the way is also from Youngstown, Ohio, although I used to play outdoor concerts with his older brothers who were both saxophone players. We would play concert band gigs in Youngstown. And I didn’t meet Harold until 1973 when we were both in New York. He had just gotten off Woody Herman’s band. So I got his number and I called him and we hooked up and had an instant friendship. We’re really good friends ‘til this day. And I started studying with him and it was perfect because I had stopped studying with Lee because basically, without saying so I think Lee had come to the point where we couldn’t, there was nothing more he could teach me or felt that he could teach me. And I felt like I still had so much to learn. And luckily I met Harold just at that moment and it was perfect because I desperately needed some basic piano chops, you know, how to voice chords, 2-5-1s and things like that. And Harold was perfect because he’s a great teacher. And he would go anywhere you wanted to go. He had no preconceived notions of anything. So he was the perfect teacher for me that I needed at precisely that moment. So I studied with him for two years and it was great. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

It seems that your career has been a series of opportunities that came up that you managed to step into and succeed. If you went to a gathering, a cocktail party or something, and it was just a brief conversation with somebody you really didn’t know and they said, “What do you do?” Do you have like a brief answer?
My elevator moment?
Thank you for, yes, that would do.
Or they say something you could tell people in the course of an elevator ride.
Yeah.
Well my stock response is I’m a saxophone player, a composer/arranger, a band leader, a jazz historian, a radio producer, a record producer, and an educator.
Okay.

That’s, all of which I’ve done — and I’d like to think that I’ve done all those things on a world class level. I mean, which is not, I’m not making myself into some kind of uber- mensch. I mean I could point to any one of those things and tell you oodles of people who do any one of those things better than I can. But nonetheless I’ve managed to do stuff in all of those categories that is on a world class level, so that’s something I’m proud of.
As you should be. And that would have gotten you to the fourth floor and that person would have learned a lot I think.
Hope so.

Yeah. What is the, what stands out in your mind — this is sort of a two part question. And people have asked me this question and I have a hard time answering, but do you recall both the worst musical situation or gig you’ve ever been in, and the best.
Oh man. Well the worst, there are so many that they’re beyond enumerating.
Really?

Well, well, well I mean in the 80s I used to do a lot of commercial gigs, club dates you know, where you would just get hired and you would just be sent out to play with some kind of ad hoc pick up band doing a wedding or a bar mitzvah or a private party. And so many of those things were just so dreadful you know, in terms of I mean the music sucked, it was frightfully loud, just everything about it was blah. So I mean there were so many of those that are beyond recall. I mean I remember some of the worst of them but the rest I’ve just kind of blanked out, just out of self defense.
Can I ask you one thing about that? Do you recall the pay scale for those, are you talking about maybe in the 80s?

Yeah. When I came back, after I went to college I went to DC for five years and was there for five years and then I came back to New York in 1980 and I started just, because it was work I made some phone calls and I started doing these club dates in addition to © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

whatever jazz playing I was doing, rehearsing with bands or playing little jazz gigs, or I started putting together my own nonet. But I remember in 1980 for a four hour Saturday night club date the scale was 96 dollars. By the time I quit doing those gigs, about in the early 90s the scale was up to about 200 dollars for a Saturday night.
And that’s a union scale?
Yeah. That’s a Local 802 club date scale for a four hour Saturday night. Four hour continuous as they say.

Now if a person, if a young woman calls you and says, “I’m getting married, I got your name, can you play” — and all the details. Is this something that you were required to go through the union to do?

No. I mean I worked, at the time there were these different club date offices that would just hire you and send you out to play with these ad hoc bands. Some of them were people that I worked with on a fairly steady basis and some of them were just one nighters, people I’d never seen before. But I would just go where I was told to go. But anyway, to answer the other part of your question, the best gigs I’ve ever done, I’m lucky in that several of them by serendipitously were recorded and have come out on CD. I mean one of them is doing the Chicago Jazz Festival in 1987 with my nonet and Sheila Jordan as a guest vocalist. I mean that’s on CD now. I sent you a link that that on YouTube. Another one is a concert that my nonet did at the Smithsonian in 1990 that is on a two CD set called “Trance Dance.” Yet another is a concert that the nonet did at the New School in 2001 that’s on CD, that’s called “Lifeline.” Still another is a duo concert that I did with Marc Copland at the New School in 2008, that’s on a CD called “Old Friends.” And then the last one is a concert at the New School in 2014 with Carlton Holmes on piano and Jim Ferguson is a great singer and bass player from Nashville and the late Holli Ross who was a wonderful singer who died a year or so ago of cancer, far too young by the way. So that’s on CD. That’s another thing called “An Evening of Indigos.” So I’ve been very lucky that some of the best nights of my career have been recorded well and are, and they came out great performance-wise, and they’re available on CD. So I’ve been exceptionally lucky in that respect.

I’m happy to hear that all the best gigs you mentioned were with your own arrangements and, you know, like sort of you being in charge. And I think that speaks well of your career also. A while back I watched a documentary on Quincy Jones. And you know I’ve been a fan, like most people, of the majority of his work and —
I saw that.

Yeah. And I may have missed it, but he never was asked where do your ideas come from. And this is sort of a follow up of the “All of Me” question that we did a half an hour ago, © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
but when you go to write an original work, or even arrangements, can you, maybe it’s an unanswerable question but can you tell me where your ideas come from?

Well in part from that pitch module process that I told you about, where I just generate some raw material you know to come up with ideas. Other times I’ve written a couple of pieces that were just from a person’s name, you know that you could play the notes on the piano and come up with a melody from a person’s name and then from that generated a melody. I just use these kind of artificial devices. And then other times they’ve just been just sheer inspiration. It varies. I’ve learned to embrace inspiration when it presents itself but when it doesn’t I’ve come up with, I’ve learned to use these kind of artificial devices that enable me to come up with raw material so that I’m not sitting there staring at the keyboard hoping for inspiration to write.
Have you ever written something then you’re like excited about it only to find out that someone else wrote it already? That you’re unconsciously channeling some other melody?
No.
Well that’s good. Because I have.

Okay. No I guess I don’t mean to sound egocentric about this but I know a hell of a lot of recorded music so the chances of something coming up that I haven’t heard or, at this point in my life, are pretty slim you know. I’ve been listening to recorded music since I was four or five years old. And I’ve checked out a lot of stuff, a huge amount of stuff. So I mean I have a very keen sense of what’s out there and what’s been done. I mean one of the things when I’m teaching jazz courses, whether it’s jazz history or composing or arranging or ensembles or whatever is that I try to give students an idea of what’s been done. I play the recordings of great whatever, of great soloing, of great writing, of, you know whatever, just so that they get a chance of what’s been done so that they’re not reinventing the wheel.
Do you ever give them assignments to purposely reinvent the wheel?
No, no. I always encourage them to do their own thing as best they can.

I think you mentioned something I read that the current generation of aspiring young jazz artists not only have to be good improvisers with their instruments, they have to improvise their career. How do we make up for the fact that the jam sessions and the small club gigs and the touring bands are mostly a thing of the past?

Well I wouldn’t say that the small club gigs, I mean there are still sessions, I mean my students here in New York, well prior to the pandemic of course, but there are still these clubs like Small’s in New York where students get together and do their little gigs and play. And there are still plenty of sessions. I mean a lot of it is now through the veneer of education I guess. And just — six horns for me was a good size. It gave you enough horns to basically duplicate just about any voicing you wanted to do, and also with having two trumpets, having the second trumpet underneath the lead trumpet makes a big difference with writing ensemble tuttis, it gives a lot of additional support that you don’t have when you only have one trumpet. So that ended up being my instrumentation of choice. And also, you know I mean it was the best of all possible worlds for me.
